::: {.r-fit-text}
Researchers share their work openly.\
AI consumes it at scale.\
[Is this a new problem, or an old one made visible?]{.rn-fragment rn-type="highlight" rn-color="#f9e4b7"}
:::

::: {.notes}
I want to start with a provocation rather than a thesis.

The tension between open scholarship and AI is real — but I don't think it's new.

☞ I think AI has made visible a set of tensions that were always present in how we think about open information commons.

This talk is about those tensions, and what a social rather than technical lens reveals about them.
:::

## Commons are social systems

::: {.fragment}
Researchers have always participated in **information commons**:

- Citing prior work, sharing data, building on others' findings
- These commons are scaffolded by [norms and commitments]{.rn-fragment rn-type="underline" rn-color="#2a6496" rn-strokeWidth=2} — not just platforms and mandates
- Instilled through participation in communities of practice
:::

::: {.fragment}
Science reform operates by implementing **new rules, new laws, new technical processes**.
:::

::: {.notes}
So what makes that kind of engagement possible? And what threatens it?

☞ Researchers have always participated in information commons — citing, sharing, building on prior work.

☞ But these commons are scaffolded by norms and commitments instilled through community membership, not just platforms or mandates.

☞ However, we are increasingly being told that opening our research requires new rules, new laws, and new technical processes - which may contradict or disrupt established norms and traditions.

While some significant changes may be warranted, they must be implemented with care.
:::

## Commons are social systems

::: {.fragment}
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Technical camp**

Infrastructures & mandates\
Information as disembodied\
Problems are legalistic in nature
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Humanistic camp**

Reforming science as inclusive\
Knowledge as socially situated\
Problems are rooted in culture
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
The technical camp dominates policy.\
[**The humanistic camp is better equipped to understand the actual problem.**]{.rn-fragment rn-type="underline" rn-color="#2a6496" rn-strokeWidth=3}
:::

::: {.notes}
☞ The open science movement has two orientations that rarely talk to each other. A technical camp designs infrastructure and mandates — FAIR data, open access requirements, licensing frameworks, whereas a humanistic camp is concerned with reforming science as a more inclusive, culturally aware enterprise.

The technical camp sees problems as legalistic: access, interoperability, reproducibility, and the humanistic camp sees problems as rooted in culture: who gets to participate, whose knowledge counts, how norms are negotiated.

☞ The technical camp dominates policy.

☞ But it's the humanistic camp is better equipped to understand the actual problem — which is why we're here today talking about AI and commons rather than just filing a complaint with a licensing body.

But before I continue, I want to be upfront about where I'm coming from.

I do use AI in my work. I use commercial tools to develop data processing pipelines that I would not otherwise be able to make, I use local models as part of extended text analysis toolchains, and I generally find it handy as a reflexive tool to enter in dialog with myself.

But I also think it's important to do these things with care and with critical thought.

I use these tools as methods, not as sources of truth, and as I'll argue here today, this makes a world of a difference.
:::

## The "no boundaries" claim is a happy lie

"Universal access" sounds egalitarian.

But even the most committed open advocates expect [**citation, attribution, appropriate reuse**]{.rn-fragment rn-type="box" rn-color="#2a6496"}.

::: {.fragment}
Commons have never been, and don't need to be, egalitarian.\
They are [**governed**]{.rn-fragment rn-type="underline" rn-color="#2a6496"} — who contributes, who accesses, in what ways.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The boundary is not a wall. It's a **sniff test** —\
[judged by behavior, care, and commitment, not credentials alone.]{.rn-fragment rn-type="underline" rn-color="#2a6496" rn-strokeWidth=2}
:::

::: {.notes}
That distinction between using tools as methods, with care, in compliance with community norms and values, is exactly what open science policy tends to flatten.

It declares "universal access" as if no conditions exist, but they always have — they're just implicit.

☞ Even open science's most committed advocates claim ownership of their creative outputs, and expect their work to be cited, engaged with charitably, and used in ways consistent with its intent.

☞ In this sense, open commons have always been ☞ governed. We actually impose strict controls over who may contribute and extract from the commons, and in what ways.

☞ The mechanism for enforcing these rules are rarely formal. It's more of a sensibility — ☞ a judgment about whether someone is engaging in good faith, with care, with some understanding of what they're working with. Credentials don't confer that. Community membership does.
:::

## Case 1: PDF piracy

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Aaron Swartz**\
Shared academic papers widely\
→ *Celebrated*
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
**Meta**\
Scraped LibGen at scale\
→ *Condemned*
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Same act. Radically different valence.
:::

::: {.fragment}
[One **serves** the community]{.rn-fragment rn-type="highlight" rn-color="#FFDE64"} — makes research available to people who can't get it any other way, and adds to the commons in doing so.
:::

::: {.fragment}
[The other **extracts** from it]{.rn-fragment rn-type="highlight" rn-color="#FF746C"} — a predatory actor in it for themselves alone.
:::

::: {.fragment}
[**The difference is relational, not technical or legal.**]{.rn-fragment rn-type="underline" rn-color="#2a6496" rn-strokeWidth=3}
:::

::: {.notes}
Aaron Swartz downloaded millions of academic papers and planned to release them publicly. The research community celebrated him for it.

☞ Meta scraped LibGen to train its models — an outside actor with nothing invested in the commons, and the community condemned them for it.

☞ Same act. Radically different valence.

☞ Swartz serves the community — makes research available to people who can't get it any other way, ☞ and adds to the commons in doing so.

☞ Meta extracts from it — ☞ a predatory actor with no stake in what it takes.

☞ The difference isn't technical. It isn't even legal. It's relational.

☞
:::

## Case 2: The Internet Archive

The National Emergency Library (2020) — granting access to books during Covid-19.

::: {.fragment}
- [Informed by professional archival principles]{.rn-fragment rn-type="highlight" rn-color="#FFDE64"} ✓
- [Driven by confidence in technical solutions to social problems]{.rn-fragment rn-type="highlight" rn-color="#FF746C"} ✗
:::

::: {.fragment}
It applied a technical resolution to an underlying social problem.\

[The manner of the intervention mattered as much as the outcome.]{.rn-fragment rn-type="underline" rn-color="#2a6496"}
:::

::: {.notes}
The Internet Archive is a more complicated case, which is why it's useful here.

☞ The archival mission is legitimate and community-serving. But the National Emergency Library was also an example of a certain tech-driven confidence: the idea that you can resolve questions of access, copyright, and distribution through unilateral technical action.

It ended in lawsuits, partly because publishers felt the Archive had overstepped — not just legally, but in terms of the norms of how decisions about access get made.

The point isn't that they were wrong to try. It's that the manner of the intervention mattered as much as the outcome.
:::

## Case 3: Big data archaeology

Archaeology produces a lot of data.\
Much of it is now publicly available.

::: {.fragment}
What happens when outsiders use it?
:::

## Case 3: Big data archaeology

Computer scientists / data scientists / physicists publish high-profile papers "solving" archaeological problems with large integrated datasets.

::: {.fragment}
| | Outside the community | Inside the community |
|--|---|---|
| Treatment of data | Neutral, abstract, recombinant | Storied, situated, context-laden |
| Epistemic stance | Data taken as source of universal truth | Contributing one point of view |
| Community response | Intuitively rejected | Treated with consideration |
:::

::: {.fragment}
[The difference is not credentials. It's **care** —\
understanding a dataset's circumstances of creation comes from community membership.]{.rn-fragment rn-type="highlight" rn-color="#FFDE64" rn.multiline=true}
:::

::: {.notes}
Any archaeologist who reads these outsider papers will feel something is wrong before they can fully articulate why.

It's because the data is being treated as neutral and abstract — as if knowing the variable names is the same as knowing what they mean.

Archaeologists know that datasets carry histories. They know that a field record reflects the decisions of a particular excavator on a particular day, under particular conditions. That knowledge comes from having been trained as an archaeologist.

When a computer scientist treats a dataset as a clean input to an algorithm, they're not doing something illegal. They're doing something epistemically careless. And the community can tell.
:::

## AI as amplifier, not origin

We put our data out there. We made it FAIR.\
We imagined certain use-cases. Certain users.

::: {.fragment}
AI scraped it for different ends.
:::

::: {.fragment}
This is structurally similar to UNESCO World Heritage claims:\
[*"for all humanity"*]{.rn-fragment rn-type="circle" rn-color="#2a6496"} — often at the expense of those who inhabit and maintain the site.
:::

::: {.fragment}
[The problem isn't AI per se.\
It's AI deployed **without community membership**]{.rn-fragment rn-type="highlight" rn-color="#FFDE64" rn.multiline="true"} — without the gradual participation that builds the tacit knowledge to use data responsibly.
:::

::: {.notes}
We did this. We built the infrastructure. We put our data out there and declared it open.

The FAIR principles — Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable — were designed with a certain kind of user in mind. Not language model training pipelines.

The UNESCO analogy is apt: when you declare something a common heritage of humanity, you create conditions for uses you never anticipated, and you can undermine the people who actually maintain the thing.

AI didn't break the commons. It exposed the gap between what we said the commons was for and what "open" actually meant in practice.
:::

---

::: {.r-fit-text}
Is AI being done by humanists,\
or by engineers playing humanist\
for an afternoon?
:::

::: {.notes}
A blanket boycott treats all AI use as equivalent — which is exactly the kind of category error I've been arguing against throughout this talk.

The question isn't whether AI is involved. It's who is doing the work, how it's being done, whether it's done with respect and care for the data and the community, and how truth claims are expressed.

Using AI locally, on device, for a specific research question, with explicit attention to its limitations — that looks very different from training a foundation model on scraped scholarship and selling access to it.
:::

## Humanities defined by practice, not data type

Humanities is not defined by the kinds of data it uses.

[It's defined by the **care and approaches** we take —\
the training, the community embedding, the commitments.]{.rn-fragment rn-type="highlight" rn-color="#FFDE64" rn.multiline="true"}

::: {.fragment}
You can't substitute a flashy method for a good question,\
a rigorous orientation, or an open mind.

[Tool-fetishizing has always been a dead end.]{.rn-fragment rn-type="underline" rn-color="#2a6496" rn-strokeWidth=3}
:::

::: {.fragment style="padding-top: 5px;"}
[Humanists are extremely well-equipped to engage with AI —\
critically, carefully, on their own terms]{.rn-fragment rn-type="highlight" rn-color="#F3A6C8" rn.multiline=true}
:::

::: {.notes}
This is ultimately a question about what makes work humanistic.

If it's the data type — text, material culture, historical sources — then AI potentially threatens the boundary by operating on the same materials.

But if it's the orientation — the care, the situatedness, the attention to how knowledge is made — then humanists are not just equipped to engage with AI, they're better equipped than most to do so critically.

We already read sources against the grain. We already ask who produced this, under what conditions, with what intentions. That's exactly what's needed when evaluating AI-generated outputs.
:::

# Where do we draw the line?

Re-defining open social scholarship is not about\
redrawing the line from scratch.

::: {.fragment}
[It's about making the existing lines more **legible** —\
more **porous** where appropriate,\
**defended** where they matter.]{.rn-fragment rn-type="highlight" rn-color="#C3B1E1" rn-multiline="true"}
:::

::: {.fragment}
The line isn't gone.\
It's [ours]{.rn-fragment rn-type="underline" rn-color="#2a6496" rn-strokeWidth=3} to tend.
:::

::: {.notes}
The conference theme asks us to re-define open social scholarship. I want to resist the word "re-define" slightly — not because definitions don't matter, but because the framing implies we're starting from scratch.

We're not. We have communities of practice. We have norms. We have commitments. AI has strained them, but it hasn't erased them.

What's needed is not new definitions but greater legibility — making explicit the implicit agreements that have always governed how we share and use scholarly work.

Thank you.
:::
